newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end lower on profit-taking after rally.
newsitem.headline: Stocks end lower on profit-taking after rally.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average ended slightly lower on profit-taking Monday as the market paused after rallying earlier in the day and racking up four record highs last week.
The Dow closed 3.36 points lower at 6,090.87 after soaring 125 points last week, ending with a record high close Friday of 6,094.23.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,306 to 1,057 on heavy volume of 414 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"It's a fairly quiet week for economic news so it's the quarterly earnings and comments surrounding them that are the news," said Charlie Crane, director of research of Spears Benzak Salomon & Farrell.
The market lurched along in fits and starts from the opening, as investors reacted to Wall Street's opinions about the third-quarter results of heavyweight International Business Machines Corp.
"The market followed IBM. It is certainly a bellwether not just for the tech sector but for corporate America," Crane said.
The Dow index topped 6,100 for the first time during Monday's session, hitting a high of 6,133.73 before falling to a session low of 6,059.94 as investors cashed out some profits.
Likewise, IBM ended up 3/4 to 130-1/8 after hitting a 52-week high of 135-3/8 vs. a session low of 126-3/4.
IBM said it earned $1.3 billion in the third quarter vs. a loss of $500 million a year ago when it was paying for its acquisition of Lotus Development Corp.
The market got an extra boost from comments by IBM's Chief Financial Officer G. Richard Thoman that he was still "very comfortable" about the firm's prospects for 1996 and its position going forward.
"The CFO's comments were encouraging and taken as a bellwether for the industry," Crane said.
Just as IBM set the tone for trading on Monday, computer software giant, Microsoft could set Tuesday's pace.

After the market closed Monday, Microsoft said its quarterly earnings rose to a record $614 million, or 95 cents a share, from $499 million, or 78 cents a share. The earnings beat Wall Street estimates of 90 cents a share.
"It's a good number. I would expect stocks to rebound tomorrow," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
Microsoft closed 3/4 lower at 134 but rallied to 136-3/8 in after-hours trading on the upbeat earnings.
"When the dust settles, most analysts will say earnings were generally better than the most recent expectations," Crane said.

"But if we backtracked six to eight weeks they were on target relative to those estimates," he said. "Year-over-year comparisons are among the weakest for five years. But the news dominating headlines are those actually registering reasonably respectable earnings."
Oil stocks were mostly flat after several big oil companies reported their results.

Texaco's profits jumped 50 percent to $434 million, while Exxon's net income was at a new high for a third quarter of $1.56 billion, topping the previous third quarter record of $1.50 billion a year ago.
Texaco rose 2-1/4 to 105-7/8, Exxon slipped 3/8 to 89 and Chevron was off 3/8 to 67-1/8, Amoco gained 1/2 to 75-3/8, while Mobil lost 1-3/8 to 119-3/4.

Among other issues, Xerox resumed its slide, losing 2-3/8 to 46-1/2 and was the most-active NYSE issue. Lehman Brothers downgraded the stock and Salomon cut earnings estimates. The stock slumped 8-1/8 Friday after reporting dismal earnings.
Sinclair Broadcast lost 9 to 34-3/4. The company warned that it would report disappointing results.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 6.07 points to 1,236.41.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks lost 0.97 to 709.85. The American Stock Exchange index was off 2.16 to 576.87.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.40 to 377.92. The average share was down 4 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 6,927.422 down 16.375 or 0.24 percent.
